newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Copyright experts try to tidy up Net ownership.
newsitem.headline: Copyright experts try to tidy up Net ownership.

text.p: Copyright experts trying to catch cyberspace pirates began talks in Geneva on Monday to tidy up legislation on who owns what on the Internet.

Copyright laws based on national boundaries have been made irrelevant by the borderless and fast world of the Internet -- a giant copying machine where anything from music to software can be duplicated and distributed at the click of a computer mouse.

The three-week conference, under the auspices of the World Intellectual Property Organisation (WIPO), a specialised U.N. coordinating body for international patents, trademarks and copyrights, is the first major revision of international copyright laws in 25 years.

Representatives from more than 120 countries will approve three new treaties -- for literary and artistic works, the rights of performers and producers of music and producers of databases -- to ensure electronic transmission of any copyrighted work is subject to the same rules as hard copies.
"Already the problems have started. They are expanding every day. We need an answer," Mihaly Ficsor, deputy director general of WIPO, told a news conference.

In favour of strict legislation are multi-billion-dollar copyright-based industries such as movie-makers, software companies and music producers which are battling to keep profits against the hi-tech information age revolution.
Allen Dixon of the Business Software Alliance said offline and online piracy had cost the software industry $4.4 billion.

"In the offline world, about one out of every two copies of software that's in use has not been authorised. On the Internet, we have pirate sites that have several thousand dollars worth of software on them which people are copying every day," he said.
"These treaties provide a basic level of protection. That's a big step forward."

A key problem facing copyright holders in the new multimedia world is that it is easy to violate copyright unintentionally. And in some cases, such as consumers of music who copy audio off the Internet, the pirate and consumer can be the same person.

Critics of the draft laws, including consumer and education groups as well as a group of U.S. online and Internet service providers, say a legal copyright superstructure lasting into the future could actually stifle the Internet.
Some U.S. providers have said that the WIPO proposals may clog public access to the system, retard the Internet and jeopardise the future of electronic communication and commerce.

Ficsor dismissed the criticism: "When service providers first saw the draft treaties, they got a bit frightened. They thought the language used would be a basis for strict liability for them. But now there is an emerging agreement," he said.
He said online servers would be liable for cases when they knew an infringement had taken place and would have to block the availability of the system and remove the infringing material.
Once the new treaties are passed, then the question will be enforcement. Distribution of copyrighted work will be illegal. But new mechanisms will be needed to catch the uploaders.
In the multimedia world of Internet and its "copyright havens", officials acknowledged there would be huge technical problems in enforcing copyright legislation.

"Which law should be applied to the Internet? Commercial laws? Private international law? How to monitor the system? Liability differs from country to country," Ficsor said. "There will always be copyright havens.
